Time to finish path P: T_P = W_P / (q · B_P)
Time to finish path H: T_H = W_H / ((1−q) · B_H)

Let me step back and think about what makes physical sense for "two resource paths finish together":

The cleanest true statement: **Two paths with remaining work R_P, R_H and current drain rates v_P, v_H finish simultaneously iff R_P/v_P = R_H/v_H.** Any law enforcing "finish together" is enforcing R_P·v_H = R_H·v_P.

Now parametrize the control knob as q with v_P = q·B_P and v_H = B_H (knob throttles P; H pinned at capacity). Then condition: R_P·B_H = R_H·q·B_P ⇒ q* = (R_P/R_H)·(B_H/B_P). With m := R_P/R_H (measured remaining-work ratio), q* = m·B_H/B_P. Inverse of target.

Parametrize with knob on H: v_P = B_P, v_H = q·B_H: R_P·q·B_H = R_H·B_P ⇒ q* = (R_H/R_P)·(B_P/B_H) = (1/m)·B_P/B_H. Target iff m := R_H/R_P.

So: **define m as the measured remaining-work ratio of H to P** (m = R_H/R_P), knob q throttles H's grant relative to its budget B_H, P runs flat-out at B_P. Then q* = m·B_P/B_H exactly. Sanity: if H has twice the remaining work (m=2) and equal budgets, q*=2 — H needs double grant to keep pace. If H's budget is huge (B_H >> B_P), q* shrinks — H barely needs any of its fat pipe. Checks out intuitively. ✓

Also nice: q* > 1 means H needs more than its nominal budget — impossible; guardrail: clamp q ≤ 1 and flag deficit, or equivalently the law detects q*_required > 1 and escalates (can't equalize without breaching H's budget; options: raise B_H, shed load from H, or accept skew). Similarly q* ≤ 0 degenerate. Also saturation floor: if m·B_P/B_H exceeds 1, the best achievable is q=1 and residual skew ΔT = R_H/B_H − R_P/B_P > 0 — measurable violation → action.
